question: A 60-year-old man on long-term immunosuppressive therapy develops thick, hyperkeratotic crusts on his hands and feet with surprisingly little itch. Two nurses on his ward have developed itchy rashes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.text: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies — highly contagious, requires isolation and combined topical permethrin plus oral ivermectin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Hyperkeratotic crusts in an immunocompromised patient with minimal itch but rapid nosocomial spread is classic crusted (Norwegian) scabies — a hyperinfestation harbouring thousands to millions of mites. It requires isolation, combined topical permethrin plus repeated oral ivermectin, and often a keratolytic to penetrate the crusts.

answers.text: Ordinary scabies — treat the patient alone with permethrin 5% cream

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The minimal itch despite thick crusts and the rapid spread to two nurses indicate a mite burden far exceeding ordinary scabies (which typically has only 10–15 mites). This is crusted scabies, requiring combined treatment, strict isolation, and treatment of all ward contacts.

answers.text: Psoriasis — the hyperkeratotic crusts in an immunocompromised patient suggest a flare

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Psoriasis can produce hyperkeratotic plaques, but it does not explain two nurses developing itchy rashes — that contact pattern is diagnostic of an infective ectoparasite. The immunocompromised state predisposes to crusted scabies, not psoriasis.

answers.text: Contact dermatitis from hospital detergents — no infection-control measures needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Contact dermatitis does not spread person-to-person. The pattern of hyperkeratotic crusts in an immunocompromised host with nosocomial transmission to healthcare workers is diagnostic of crusted scabies, which demands immediate infection-control measures.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: hyperkeratotic crusts + immunosuppression + minimal itch + contact spread = crusted (Norwegian) scabies. The paradoxically low itch reflects impaired type IV hypersensitivity, while the massive mite burden (millions vs the usual 10–15) drives extreme contagiousness.

Crusted scabies is one of the most important diagnoses in hospital dermatology — the massive mite burden makes it a nosocomial hazard. Always suspect it when an immunocompromised patient has hyperkeratotic crusts with contacts developing itch.
